[00:00] [ Music ] GEORGIA KALYVA: How do you prove an AI solution is worth the investment before committing budget, resources, and long-term support? Hi and welcome. I'm Georgia, Lead Technical Trainer at Microsoft, and in this session we'll see practical tools you need to justify AI investments, earn stakeholder trust, and ensure your solutions deliver real measurable value.

[00:30] Let's get started. By the end of this video, you will be able to define ROI criteria, evaluate the total cost of ownership, build a solid ROI analysis, decide whether to build or buy or extend AI components, and implement model routing strategies. These are not just theoretical concepts. Whether you are new to AI or a seasoned architect, this module gives you a structured framework to make smarter AI decisions.

[01:03] Let's start with selecting the right ROI or return on investment criteria for AI-powered business solutions, including total cost of ownership. Whether you are working with Copilot Studio agents, Microsoft 365 Copilot extensions, or custom AI workflows, every solution needs a rigorous ROI evaluation. As an agentic AI architect, your job is to capture not just financial impact, but also productivity gains, risk reduction, and the full lifecycle cost.

[01:36] Here is a reality check: AI adoption often does not happen, and it is usually not because the technology does not work. It fails when organizations overestimate productivity gains, underestimate ongoing maintenance costs, lack clear measurement frameworks, or simply cannot articulate business value to leadership. Sounds familiar? That is why defining ROI criteria up front is so important.

[02:04] Your ROI approach must be measurable, repeatable, aligned to business outcomes, and grounded in real usage analytics. As an agentic AI architect, your best practice is to set realistic expectations from Day 1 and tie every AI initiative to concrete, trackable metrics. This protects both the project and your credibility. Let's talk about productivity gains, the first of five core ROI categories.

[02:34] This is often the most visible benefit of AI. Think about time saved per task, reduction in manual data entry, faster case resolution, and automated summarization or classification. These are the kinds of improvements that people notice right away. The key best practice here is to use built-in analytics to track time saved, per session, task automation rates, and user adoption metrics to not just estimate -- measure.

[03:04] As an agentic AI architect, always ground your productivity claims in real telemetry data. Assumptions are the enemy of credibility when you are presenting to leadership. Make every number defensible. Next come cost savings. This is where AI starts speaking the language of finance. We are talking about reduced labor hours, lower operational overhead, decreased support ticket volume, and reduced manual review or compliance workload.

[03:38] Built-in ROI dashboards can estimate cost savings per automated task per user and aggregate savings over time. Here is the best practice: Always calculate cost savings alongside productivity gains, not instead of them. They reinforce each other. As an AI architect, think of cost savings as your bridge to the CFO.

[04:03] When you control dollars saved per task multiplied by thousands of tasks, this is when budgets get approved. Revenue impact is the third ROI category, and honestly, it is the one that gets executives most excited. We are talking about increased sales conversion, faster lead qualification, improved customer retention, and upsell or cross-sell recommendations powered by AI.

[04:34] This category can be harder to measure directly, but it is incredibly powerful. The best practice is to connect your AI solution to specific revenue-generating outcomes, not just efficiency. As an agentic AI architect, always ask how does this solution help the organization make more money, not just save money? That dual lens of cost reduction plus revenue growth makes your business case nearly unbeatable.

[05:05] Risk reduction is our fourth ROI category, and it is one that often gets overlooked: fewer compliance violations, reduced error rates, improved data consistency, and lower operational risk. These might not grab headlines, but they can save organizations millions in fines, rework, and reputational damage. Risk reduction is a first-class ROI driver, not an afterthought.

[05:32] As an AI architect, build risk metrics into every evaluation from the start. Think about what happens when things go wrong without AI. The cost of errors, compliance breaches, and inconsistent data adds up fast. Quantifying risk avoided is just as important as quantifying time saved. The fifth and final ROI category is strategic and innovation value.

[06:01] This one is about the bigger picture: new business models, enhanced customer experience, and competitive differentiation. These benefits are harder to put a dollar figure on, but they are often the most transformative. Think beyond immediate returns. As an agentic AI architect, your best practice is to frame strategic value as optionality. AI does not just solve today's problems.

[06:26] It opens doors to capabilities your organization could not have before. When you present ROI, include this forward-looking dimension. It helps stakeholders see AI as a long-term investment, not just a cost center. Now we shift to total cost of ownership, and this is where many AI projects get into trouble.

[06:52] TCO answers a fundamentally different question than ROI. ROI asks what you get back. TCO asks what you spend across the entire AI life cycle. Development costs are your starting point: data preparation, prompt engineering, agent design and testing, and integration with business systems. Here is the critical best practice: Never treat the initial build cost as the total investment.

[07:21] Studies show organizations routinely underestimate AI project costs by more than 10%, and many miss by over 25%. As an AI architect, your job is to surface the true cost picture from Day 1. Deployment costs are the second TCO category, and they are often where hidden expenses start piling up. Infrastructure provisioning, licensing, security, and compliance setup, and API usage costs -- these can scale unexpectedly, especially with usage-based pricing models.

[07:58] This is what catches many teams off guard. API costs that look manageable during a pilot can multiply dramatically at production scale. The best practice is to model your deployment costs at full scale, not just at pilot volume. As an agentic AI architect, always build headroom into your cost estimates for security, compliance, and infrastructure scaling. Better to overbudget and come in under than to face a surprise overrun.

[08:30] Operational costs are the third TCO category, and they are the ones that keep running long after launch: monitoring and evaluation, model retraining, prompt library maintenance, support and troubleshooting, and user training, and adoption programs. AI is not a set-it-and-forget-it technology. Models drift. Prompts need updating. Users need ongoing training.

[08:55] Your best practice is to budget 20-30% of your initial development cost annually for ongoing operations. Factor in continuous improvement cycles from the start. The organizations that succeed with AI are the ones that plan for the long run, not just launch. Change management costs are the fourth TCO category, and this is the one most frequently skipped in AI business cases.

[09:23] Scaling and enablement, communication and rollout, business process redesign -- getting the technology right is only half the battle. Getting people to actually adopt and use it effectively is the other half. Change management is not optional; it's essential. As an agentic AI architect, budget real time and money for training, internal communications, and process redesign. The best AI solution in the world delivers zero value if nobody uses it.

[09:53] Make adoption a first-class line item in every TCO model you built. Decommissioning costs round out our TCO picture, retiring outdated models and migrating to new architectures. [10:20] The model you deploy today may need to be replaced in 18 to 24 months. Your best practice is to design for portability from the start. Avoid deep vendor lock-in where possible, document your architecture thoroughly, and plan migration paths early. The total in TCO means total from the beginning to end.
